name: Battle of Agincourt
info: On 25 October 1415 Henry V's English army, marching to Calais and heavily outnumbered, defeated a French army near Azincourt in northern France, a victory that gave England the advantage in the Hundred Years' War for some years.

facts.place: Near Azincourt in northern France, on open land between the woods of Tramecourt and Azincourt; the exact site is disputed
facts.sides: English army under King Henry V, about 9,000 men at the march from Harfleur, of whom about 1,500 men-at-arms and 7,000 longbowmen were deployed; French army under Constable Charles I d'Albret, 14,000 to 15,000 (10,000 men-at-arms and 4,000 to 5,000 other troops). Historians dispute both sets of figures.
facts.outcome: A large French force was defeated: around 6,000 French fighting men were killed and 700 to 2,200 taken prisoner, against English losses stated variously from 112 to 1,600. Henry returned to England on 16 November.

t: The English, weakened by disease and short of food after the siege of Harfleur, were blocked on the march to Calais and fought on ground chosen by Henry, a narrow, muddy field between woods.

Historians disagree about the numbers: Anne Curry's study of administrative records gives the French and English in proportions of about four to three, while others hold that the English were outnumbered several times over.
Henry ordered the killing of most French prisoners at some point in the battle, fearing a French return to the fight, while sparing the highest ranked for ransom.
dyk: The Burgundian sources have Henry telling his men that the French had boasted of cutting two fingers from the right hand of every archer. Whether this was true is open to question and is still debated.
ev: Henry V's negotiations with the French over his claims and a marriage to Catherine, daughter of Charles VI, break down
On 13 August Henry's army lands in northern France and besieges Harfleur, which surrenders on 22 September
The English leave Harfleur on 8 October and march towards Calais, forced south by French blocking of the Somme
On 24 October the two armies face each other but the French decline battle
On 25 October the English advance, the French cavalry charge fails and the French men-at-arms are defeated
Henry orders most of the French prisoners killed, sparing only the highest ranked
Henry returns to England on 16 November and is received in London on the 23rd
Within ten days of the battle the truce between the Armagnacs and Burgundians breaks down, giving Henry eighteen months to prepare a new campaign

sections.background:
The Battle of Agincourt belongs to the Hundred Years' War (1337 to 1453). Henry V claimed the title of King of France through his great-grandfather Edward III, although English kings had generally been ready to renounce it if the French recognised the English claim to Aquitaine and other lands under the terms of the Treaty of Brétigny. In 1414 Henry offered to give up the claim if the French paid the 1.6 million crowns outstanding from the ransom of John II, captured at Poitiers in 1356, and conceded Anjou, Brittany, Flanders, Normandy, Touraine and Aquitaine. He would also marry Charles VI's daughter Catherine with a dowry of 2 million crowns. The French offered a dowry of 600,000 crowns and an enlarged Aquitaine. The English felt the French had mocked their claims, and on 19 April 1415 the Great Council agreed to war.

Henry's army landed on 13 August 1415. The army of about 12,000 men and up to 20,000 horses besieged Harfleur, which surrendered on 22 September, and the army did not leave until 8 October. It had suffered many casualties from disease. Rather than retire to England, Henry decided to march most of his army, roughly 9,000, through Normandy to Calais, to show that his right to rule in the duchy was more than an abstract claim, and as a provocation to the dauphin, who had not answered his challenge to personal combat at Harfleur. The French moved to block the Somme and forced Henry south to find a ford, which the English crossed south of Péronne. By 24 October both armies faced each other, but the French declined battle, hoping for more troops.
sections.forces:
On the morning of 25 October Henry deployed his army, approximately 1,500 men-at-arms and 7,000 longbowmen, across a 750-yard (690 m) part of the defile. English and Welsh archers made up nearly 80 percent of the army. The king led the centre, Edward, Duke of York the right wing and Baron Thomas Camoys the left, and Sir Thomas Erpingham commanded the archers. The archers drove pointed stakes into the ground at an angle to turn aside cavalry. The English had very little food, had marched 260 miles (420 km) in two and a half weeks and were suffering from dysentery.

King Charles VI did not command the French army because he suffered from psychotic illnesses. It was led by Constable Charles I d'Albret and noblemen of the Armagnac party. The French are counted at 10,000 men-at-arms and some 4,000 to 5,000 miscellaneous foot soldiers (archers, crossbowmen and shield-bearers), totalling 14,000 to 15,000, and each man-at-arms was probably accompanied by an armed servant, which some historians leave out of the count. The French formed a vanguard of 4,800 men-at-arms and a main battle of 3,000, with 600 dismounted men-at-arms on each wing. A cavalry force of 800 to 1,200, under Clignet de Bréban and Louis de Bosredon, was to break the English archers, and some 200 mounted men were to attack the English rear. Many lords demanded places at the front for glory and ransoms, so the bulk of the men-at-arms were massed in front and the archers and crossbowmen were placed behind them. The rearguard on horseback was leaderless.
sections.course:
For three hours after sunrise there was no fighting. The French were expecting thousands more men and blocked Henry's retreat. Henry had to halt the retreat and engage them before the French were reinforced, so his archers pulled up their stakes, carried them forward and set them again. The French cavalry, disorganised and not at full numbers, charged only after the English began shooting. It could not outflank the archers because of the woodland nor pass the stakes. John Keegan argues that the longbows' main effect was to injure horses, which galloped back through the advancing infantry.

The French men-at-arms advanced through recently ploughed, muddy ground, with visors down against the arrows, in armour weighing 50 to 60 pounds (23 to 27 kg). Modern historians are divided on how well longbows pierced plate armour of the time. The French reached the English line and pushed it back at first, but became so tightly packed that men in the third rank could hardly use their swords. Knights who fell found it hard to rise. When the archers ran out of arrows they dropped their bows and attacked with hatchets, swords and mallets. The fighting lasted about three hours, and the leaders of the second line were killed or captured as those of the first had been. English accounts say Henry fought hand to hand and stood over his wounded brother Humphrey, receiving an axe blow to the head. Ysembart d'Azincourt, with a small number of men-at-arms and about 600 peasants, attacked the English baggage train and took some of Henry's treasures.
sections.aftermath:
At some point after the first victory Henry became alarmed that the French were regrouping and ordered most of the French prisoners killed, possibly thousands, sparing only the highest ranked, who were most likely to fetch a ransom. Most chroniclers say he feared that the prisoners, who outnumbered their captors, would rearm from the weapons on the field. Contemporary chroniclers did not criticise him. The English knights refused to take part because they thought it unchivalrous. Keegan argues that the aim was to terrorise the prisoners and that relatively few were killed before the French reserves fled and Henry rescinded the order.

Around 6,000 French fighting men were killed, among them 90 to 120 lords and bannerets, including the dukes of Alençon, Bar and Brabant, nine counts and the Constable d'Albret. According to the heralds 3,069 knights and squires died and at least 2,600 more bodies lacked coats of arms. Estimates of prisoners vary between 700 and 2,200, among them the dukes of Orléans and Bourbon. For the English, records identify at least 112 killed, Monstrelet reported 600, and Jean de Wavrin 1,600 of all ranks; the dead included the Duke of York. Henry returned to England on 16 November and entered London on the 23rd. Within ten days the Armagnac and Burgundian factions broke their truce and the Burgundians marched on Paris, giving Henry eighteen months to prepare.
sections.sources:
The battle is documented by at least seven contemporary accounts, three from eyewitnesses. Jean Le Fèvre de Saint-Remy, a Burgundian who was present, and the anonymous Gesta Henrici Quinti, believed to be by a chaplain in the king's household who would have been in the baggage train, are eyewitnesses; Enguerrand de Monstrelet, also Burgundian, is the other frequently used account, and the monk of Saint-Denis is quoted for the French side. After the battle the heralds of both armies, with Montjoie, settled the name Azincourt. Curry and Mortimer question the Gesta's reliability, noting doubts about how far it was written as propaganda for Henry V, and Mortimer thinks it overstates both French numbers and English losses at Harfleur.

The site is uncertain. It may lie on the strip between Tramecourt and Azincourt, but the lack of archaeological evidence there has led to suggestions of a site to the west, a case Michael Livingston made in 2019. The numbers are disputed. Most primary sources have the English outnumbered several times. Anne Curry, from administrative records, argued for 12,000 French and 9,000 English; Juliet Barker, Jonathan Sumption and Clifford Rogers say the English probably had 6,000 (5,000 archers and 900 to 1,000 men-at-arms) and that Curry's records are incomplete. Ian Mortimer calls 15,000 French against 8,000 to 9,000 English the most extreme imbalance that is credible. Rogers reckons the French at 24,000 counting armed servants; Barker holds that the English were outnumbered at least four to one. Historians disagree less about French numbers.
sections.legacy:
Agincourt, with Crécy and Poitiers, stands among England's great victories in the Hundred Years' War. It began a period of English dominance that lasted until 1429 and the Siege of Orléans. The victory was militarily decisive, but its impact was complex. Henry returned a conquering hero, seen as blessed by God in the eyes of his subjects and European powers outside France. The victory established the legitimacy of the Lancastrian monarchy and of his later campaigns, and the damage to Normandy's political and military structures made them easier. The French suffered a catastrophic defeat; entire noble families were wiped out in the male line, and Barker writes that the battle cut a great swath through French society in Artois, Ponthieu, Normandy and Picardy.

Songs followed soon, the best known the Agincourt Carol of the first half of the 15th century. The best-known depiction is Shakespeare's Henry V (1599), whose St Crispin's Day speech has Henry urging a band of brothers. Shakespeare's casualty figures, 10,000 French and fewer than thirty English, are not historical, and the play shows Henry's order to kill prisoners as a break with chivalry. Films from 1944, 1989 and 2019 draw on the play. The battle was likened to the British Expeditionary Force's stand at the start of the First World War. A museum, the Centre Azincourt 1415, stands in the village.

summary: On 25 October 1415 Henry V's weakened army, blocked on its way to Calais, defeated a larger French army in a narrow, muddy field near Azincourt. The French lost thousands of fighting men and many of their leaders, and the numbers on each side are still disputed.
notes: Numbers: the article gives English at about 9,000 for the march, 1,500 men-at-arms and 7,000 longbowmen in deployment, and a separate section where Barker, Sumption and Rogers say 6,000. I gave both, attributed. French: 14,000-15,000 (article's count), Rogers 24,000 counting armed servants, Curry 12,000. Not reconciled, as the article does not.
The article says 'Barker, following the Gesta, concluded that the baggage attack happened at the start'; other accounts put it near the end; I gave the attack without a time in the course section.
I did not give the French prisoners' total killed: the article says 'possibly numbering in the thousands' and Keegan thinks relatively few; both stated.
The article has Monstrelet on English dead as 600 and Wavrin as 1,600; both given. 'At least 112' is the article's record evidence.
The article uses 'catastrophic' and 'annihilated' for the French defeat; I used 'catastrophic' once, attributed as the article's own wording, and dropped 'annihilated'.
The facts 'place' says 'dispute' per the article; the article does not name present-day region beyond 'northern France'.

Left out: the Crispin speech's content beyond naming, Shakespeare's film details, the three heaps of the slain, Henry's speech, the French monk's mud descriptions beyond one, the wiki's list of notable examples in music.
